COMPLETE EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  

──────────────────────────────────────────  

1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Staggered Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event-study extension, supplemented by an IV version of DID (“legalization × cohort” as an instrument for realized abortion exposure).

Why it fits  
• Treatment rolled out at different times—five “early-legal” states in 1970, the rest after Roe in 1973—so we can compare early and late adopters before and after legalization.  
• Panel data for 51 units over 25-plus years allow 2-way fixed-effects DID, controlling for all time-invariant state factors and common national shocks.  
• We care about the cumulative effect on cohorts that reach crime-prone ages 15–24; lagging abortion exposure by cohort year maps naturally to the DID framework.  
• IV add-on mitigates endogeneity of abortion rates that may arise from contemporaneous state policies or demand shocks unrelated to legalization.  

Equation (baseline):  

Crime_rate_{st} = β AbortionExposure_{st} + γ_s + δ_t + X'_{st}θ + ε_{st}  

where AbortionExposure_{st} = Σ_{k=15}^{24} w_k AbortionRate_{s,t-k}.  

Event-study: replace AbortionExposure_{st} with dummies for event time r = year-of-birth relative to legalization to test pre-trends.  

2. Treatment and Control  
Treatment variable  
• Continuous: “effective abortion exposure” in state s, year t – a weighted average of abortion rates in the birth years of individuals aged 15-24 in year t.  

Control group / counterfactual  
• States not yet legally offering abortion by the relevant conception year provide the counterfactual path of crime.  
• In event-study plots, leads (-5 to ‑1) serve as within-state counterfactuals to test parallel trends.  

Treatment timing  
• Early-legal states: 1970.  
• All others: 1973 (Roe).  

(If IV is used) First-stage: Legalization_{s,τ} (1 if abortion is legal in state s at birth year τ) predicts AbortionRate_{s,τ}.  

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
A1. Parallel pre-trends: In the absence of legalization-induced abortion, crime trends in early- and late-legal states would have moved similarly. Plausibility: no obvious contemporaneous crime policy shock in exactly 1970 that only hit the five early states; can be visually and statistically tested with leads in event-study.  

A2. No time-varying omitted variables correlated with both abortion and future crime after controlling for X_{st}, γ_s, and δ_t. Plausible but must control for policing, incarceration, economic conditions, alcohol, welfare, immigration, gun laws.  

A3. Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA): Legal abortion access in one state does not alter crime outcomes in another via large migration flows of pregnant women. Some cross-border abortions occurred (NY, CA) → robustness: drop border counties / construct destination-state exposure.  

A4. Cohort-specific exposure correctly measured: AbortionRate_{s,t-k} uses state of occurrence; if many women travel, measurement error may attenuate β but not bias it upward.  

A5 (IV only). Exclusion restriction: Early-legalization dummy affects later crime only through its impact on abortion rates, not through contemporaneous social liberalism that independently reduces crime 15-20 years later. Test by controlling for contemporaneous ’70s policies and by placebo on older cohorts.  

4. Main Threats and Mitigation  

Threat 1: Differential pre-trends in crime or fertility.  
• Mitigation: Event-study with 5–7 leads; include state-specific linear time trends; allow state-specific cohort trends.  

Threat 2: Migration / cross-state abortion travel blurs treatment.  
• Mitigation: (i) Use Guttmacher “state-of-occurrence” but also recompute exposure using CDC “state-of-residence” where available. (ii) Exclude states bordering early-legal states; (iii) instrument exposure with legalization dummy, which is not affected by travel.  

Threat 3: Other simultaneous policy shocks (e.g., 1970 NY Rockefeller drug laws, 1970 CA sentencing reform).  
• Mitigation: Add controls for incarceration rate, police per capita, gun, alcohol, welfare, drug enforcement; perform difference-in-differences-in-event-time test on placebo cohorts aged 26-35 who were already born when legalization occurred.  

5. R Code Outline  

```r
# --- 5.1 Load packages ----
library(data.table)   # fast manipulation
library(fixest)       # high-dim FE estimation
library(ggplot2)

# --- 5.2 Read data ----
crime    <- fread("state_crime_1973_1997.csv")     # crime rates
abortion <- fread("state_abortion_1968_1997.csv")  # abortion per 1000 live births
controls <- fread("state_controls_1970_1997.csv")  # econ & policy controls

# --- 5.3 Merge to state-year panel ----
panel <- Reduce(function(x,y) merge(x,y, by = c("state","year"), all = TRUE),
                list(crime, abortion, controls))

# --- 5.4 Construct effective abortion exposure (ages 15-24) ----
# Weights: share of arrests at each age; approximate equal weights if unknown.
age_weights <- data.table(age = 15:24, w = 1/10)

# Shift abortion rates k years back and weight
for(k in 15:24){
  panel[, paste0("abort_lag_",k) := shift(abort_rate, n = k, type = "lag"),
        by = state]
}

panel[, abort_exposure := rowSums(.SD * age_weights$w, na.rm = TRUE),
      .SDcols = paste0("abort_lag_",15:24)]

# --- 5.5 Estimation: baseline TWFE ----
fe_formula <- violent_crime_rate ~ abort_exposure + prisoners_pc +
              police_pc + income_pc + unemployment + poverty +
              afdc_lag + beer_pc + immigrant_share +
              i(year) | state

mod1 <- feols(fe_formula, data = panel, cluster = "state")
summary(mod1)

# --- 5.6 Event-study (leads/lags up to 20 years) ----
# Event time = birth year relative to legalization year
legal_year <- panel[, .(legal_year = min(year[abort_legal == 1])), by = state]
panel <- merge(panel, legal_year, by = "state")

panel[, event_time := (year - legal_year) - 15] # 0 = cohort age 15 in year t

mod_es <- feols(violent_crime_rate ~ sunab(event_time, treat = (event_time>=0)) +
                prisoners_pc + police_pc + ... | state + year,
                data = panel, cluster = "state")
iplot(mod_es)

# --- 5.7 Robustness: drop border states to early-legal states ----
early <- c("Alaska","California","Hawaii","New York","Washington DC","Washington")
border_states <- c("Oregon","Nevada",...)  # fill in
panel_rb <- panel[!state %in% border_states]
mod_rb <- update(mod1, data = panel_rb)

# Compare
etable(mod1, mod_rb, tex = FALSE)
```

6. Expected Results  
Theory: Children most likely to be aborted (to very young, single, low-income mothers) are also those with the highest baseline risk of later criminal involvement. Legal access should therefore (i) reduce cohort size and (ii) improve the average “wantedness” and prenatal/early-life conditions of the marginal born child, lowering per-capita offending. I expect:  
• β < 0.  
• Magnitude: a one-standard-deviation increase in effective abortion exposure (≈ 200 abortions per 1,000 live births) lowers violent crime rates by roughly 5–10 percent 15-20 years later.  

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (Difference-in-Differences)  
C1 Parallel pre-trends visually/statistically supported…………… 0.8  
C2 No differential time-varying confounders………………………… 0.6  
C3 Accurate treatment timing & definition………………………… 0.9  
C4 No interference (SUTVA)………………………………………………… 0.6  
C5 Robust standard errors / clustering correctly done…………… 1.0  

Overall: Credible but not bullet-proof; main weaknesses are potential spillovers and remaining unobserved co-policies.
